title: Counting with indicators
objectives: Find an expected count by summing indicator variables.
Skip the full distribution of a count when only its expectation is asked

screens.title: Count the sixes
screens.prose: Here are ten rolls of a fair die. The top row shows each face. The bottom row is empty for now.
screens.question: Tap every roll that shows a six.

hints.text: Look along the top row for the face 6.
There is one six in the first two rolls.
Rolls 2, 5 and 8 show a six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the rolls whose face is 6, and only those.

byKey.two: You found two of the sixes. Look further along the row.

explain.text: Write 1 under each six and 0 under every other roll. The number of sixes is then the sum of the bottom row: $0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 3$. A count is a sum of 0s and 1s.

screens.title: Many runs of ten
screens.prose: Each run rolls ten dice and counts the sixes. Run the experiment many times and watch the average count.

derive.caption: {{ran ? 'Average number of sixes over ' + ran + ' runs: ' + fixed((1 * values.x1 + 2 * values.x2 + 3 * values.x3 + 4 * values.x4 + 5 * values.x5 + 6 * values.x6 + 7 * values.x7 + 8 * values.x8 + 9 * values.x9 + 10 * values.x10) / ran, 2) : 'Each run rolls 10 dice and counts the sixes'}}

screens.question: Where does the average number of sixes settle?

options.why: 1 is the most common count, but 2, 3 and more pull the average above it.
That is the chance of a six on one roll. A run has ten rolls.
Run 1,000 and read the caption. The average sits below 2.

hints.text: Run 1,000 and read the caption.
Compare the average with $10 \times \tfrac{1}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 and read the average in the caption.

explain.text: Over 1,000 runs the average count settles near 1.67, although no run ever has 1.67 sixes. That is $10 \times \tfrac{1}{6}$: ten rolls, each a six one time in six.

screens.title: One indicator per roll
screens.prose: A 0-or-1 variable that marks whether an event happens is an **indicator**. Let $I_k$ mark a six on roll $k$. The count is $N = I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_{10}$.
screens.question: Each $E[I_k] = \tfrac{1}{6}$, as in the long-run average lesson. Use linearity: what is $E[N]$?

widget.label: Expected number of sixes
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{10}{6}$, such as 1.67

hints.text: Linearity turns the expected count into a sum of ten expected values.
$E[N] = \tfrac{1}{6} + \dots + \tfrac{1}{6}$, ten times.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten expected values $E[I_k]$.

byKey.one: That is one indicator. The count adds ten of them.
byKey.mode: That is the most likely count. The expected count is the average.
byKey.ten: You gave every indicator expected value 1. Each roll is a six only one time in six.

explain.text: $E[N] = E[I_1] + \dots + E[I_{10}] = 10 \times \tfrac{1}{6} \approx 1.67$. We never needed $P(N = 3)$ or any other value of the pmf of $N$. Each indicator's chance was enough.

screens.title: Business cards in a bowl
screens.prose: Five traders drop their business cards in a bowl. Each draws one card at random. Let $N$ count the traders who draw their own card.

state.caption: Shaded: a trader draws their own card

screens.question: What is $E[N]$?

hints.text: Give trader A an indicator: 1 if A draws their own card.
A's own card is one of five equally likely cards.
Each of the five indicators has expected value $\tfrac{1}{5}$. Add five of them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one trader's chance, then add it over all five traders.

byKey.one: That is one trader's chance. Add it up over all five.
byKey.all: That is the chance that everyone draws their own card. The question asks for the expected count.
byKey.five: You gave each trader a certain match. Each draws their own card only one time in five.

explain.text: $E[N] = 5 \times \tfrac{1}{5} = 1$. The indicators are dependent: if four traders hold their own cards, so does the fifth. Linearity does not care, so the answer is 1 for 5 traders or for 500.

screens.title: Certain events
screens.prose: Back to ten rolls of a die. Let $M$ count the rolls that show a number from 1 to 6.

state.caption: The bottom row now marks a face from 1 to 6

screens.question: What is $E[M]$?

hints.text: What is the chance that one roll shows a number from 1 to 6?
Every indicator is 1 with chance 1. Add ten of them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each roll shows a number from 1 to 6 for certain.

byKey.sixes: That counts sixes. Every roll shows a number from 1 to 6.
byKey.one: You gave one roll. All ten rolls count.

explain.text: Each indicator is 1 for certain, so $E[M] = 10 \times 1 = 10$. A count of rolls showing a 7 would have every indicator 0, so its expected value is 0. Every expected count lies between 0 and the number of events.

screens.title: Shared birthdays
screens.prose: A room holds 23 people. Each birthday is equally likely to be any of 365 days, independently of the others. Each pair of people gets an indicator: 1 if they share a birthday.

state.caption: 6 people make 15 pairs, one line each

screens.question: What is the expected number of pairs that share a birthday? Give three decimal places.

hints.text: How many pairs can 23 people form?
6 people make 15 pairs, one per line.
$\binom{23}{2} = 253$ pairs, each sharing a birthday with chance $\tfrac{1}{365}$. Compute $\tfrac{253}{365}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs, then multiply by one pair's chance.

byKey.people: You gave each person an indicator. A shared birthday belongs to a pair, and 23 people form 253 pairs.
byKey.ordered: You counted each pair twice, as Ann with Bo and Bo with Ann. There are $23 \times 22 / 2 = 253$ pairs.
byKey.at-least-one: That is the chance of at least one shared birthday, from Counting and Chance. The question asks for the expected number of pairs.

explain.text: $E = \binom{23}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{365} = \tfrac{253}{365} \approx 0.693$. The pair indicators are dependent: if Ann matches Bo and Bo matches Cai, then Ann matches Cai. Linearity adds them anyway.

screens.title: A shuffled deck
screens.prose: A deck of 52 cards is shuffled thoroughly. A card is a match if it ends up in the same position it started in.
screens.question: How many matches do you expect?

options.text: First you need the chance of exactly 0, 1, 2, … matches
options.why: You set out to find the whole distribution of the count. That is hard and not needed: each card is a match with chance $\tfrac{1}{52}$.

options.text: It cannot be done by adding: the matches are dependent
options.why: Linearity needs no independence. Dependent indicators add just as well.
That is one card's chance. There are 52 cards.

hints.text: Give each card an indicator.
Card $k$ is a match with chance $\tfrac{1}{52}$. Add 52 of these.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one indicator's expected value over the 52 cards.

byKey.dist: You went for the full distribution of the count. Only the expectation is asked, and indicators give it in one line.
byKey.dependent: You refused to add dependent indicators. Linearity never needs independence.

explain.text: Card $k$ lands in its own position with chance $\tfrac{1}{52}$, so $E[\text{matches}] = 52 \times \tfrac{1}{52} = 1$. The full distribution is messy, yet the expectation took one line. When only an expectation is asked, sum the indicators and stop.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Every count you met was a sum of indicators. If $N = I_1 + \dots + I_n$, where $I_k$ is 1 when event $A_k$ happens, then $$E[N] = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \dots + P(A_n).$$ The events may depend on each other.
screens.question: Why is $E[I_k] = P(A_k)$?

options.text: $I_k$ is 1 with chance $P(A_k)$ and 0 otherwise, so $E[I_k] = 1 \cdot P(A_k) + 0$

options.why: Independence plays no part. The value 1 times its chance gives $P(A_k)$ on its own.

options.text: Because an indicator's expected value is always $\tfrac{1}{2}$
options.why: That holds only for an event with chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. A six has chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

hints.text: Write the pmf of one indicator.
It is 1 with chance $P(A_k)$ and 0 with chance $1 - P(A_k)$.

feedback.correct: The 0 term vanishes and leaves the chance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the values 1 and 0 by their chances.

explain.text: $E[I_k] = 1 \cdot P(A_k) + 0 \cdot (1 - P(A_k)) = P(A_k)$, the edge case from the long-run average lesson. Add these over $k$ and you have the expected count.

screens.title: The derivation
screens.prose: Put the indicator method together, one justified step per line. $N$ counts which of the events $A_1, \dots, A_n$ happen.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $N = I_1 + I_2 + \dots + I_n$, writing the count as a sum of indicators
$E[N] = E[I_1] + E[I_2] + \dots + E[I_n]$, by linearity, which needs no independence
$= \sum_k \big(1 \cdot P(A_k) + 0 \cdot P(\text{not } A_k)\big)$, from the pmf of each indicator

hints.text: Start by writing the count itself.
Linearity comes before any indicator's pmf is used.
Count, linearity, each indicator's pmf, then the sum of chances.

feedback.correct: Count, linearity, indicator pmf, sum of chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the count as a sum first, then take expected values.

byKey.d2: Linearity needs the count written as a sum first.
byKey.d3: Each $E[I_k]$ appears only after linearity splits $E[N]$.

explain.text: Line 2 is linearity, and it never asks whether the events are independent. Line 3 is the fact from the long-run average lesson that an indicator's expected value is its chance. Together they turn any expected count into a sum of chances.

screens.title: Resting limit orders
screens.prose: A trader rests 10 buy limit orders below the market. A sharp drop fills many of them at once. The table gives each order's chance of filling today.
screens.question: How many fills does the trader expect today?

hints.text: Give each order an indicator.
The expected count is the sum of the last column.

feedback.correct: The ten fill chances add to 4.65.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the ten fill chances.

byKey.half: You treated every order as a 50-50 fill. Each has its own chance.
byKey.avg: That is the average chance per order. Multiply by 10, or just add the chances.
byKey.all: You assumed every order fills. Most have a modest chance.

explain.text: Each order's indicator has expected value equal to its fill chance, so $E[\text{fills}] = 4.65$. Clustering makes 0 or 10 fills more likely than if the orders filled independently. The expected count stays 4.65.

screens.title: Defaults in a loan book
screens.prose: A bank holds 50 loans. Each defaults this year with chance 0.04. In a recession, defaults come together.
screens.question: What is the expected number of defaults this year?

options.why: Clustering widens the spread: some years see none, some see many. The average stays at $50 \times 0.04 = 2$.

options.text: It cannot be found without the correlation
options.why: The correlation is needed for the spread of the count, not for its expected value.
That is one loan's chance. Add it over 50 loans.

hints.text: Give each loan an indicator.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 50 default chances.

byKey.more: You let the clustering move the average. It changes how bad a bad year is, not the expected count.

explain.text: $E[\text{defaults}] = 50 \times 0.04 = 2$, whatever the correlation. The correlation decides how often a bad year brings 10 defaults, which is the risk a bank holds capital for. The Correlated defaults lesson in Conditional Probability shows how one default raises the chance of another.

ideas: Write a count as a sum of indicators, one for each event that might happen.
The expected count is the sum of the events' chances, even when the events depend on each other.
When only the expectation is asked, skip the full distribution of the count.

formula.name: Expected count
formula.note: $N$ counts which of the events $A_1, \dots, A_n$ happen.

summary.trap: Hunting for the distribution of a count, or refusing to add because the events are dependent.

quiz.prose: A biased coin shows heads with chance 0.3. You toss it 20 times.
quiz.question: How many heads do you expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one toss's chance of heads over 20 tosses.

byKey.fair: You treated the coin as fair. Heads has chance 0.3.
byKey.one: That is one toss. There are 20.

explain.text: One indicator per toss, each with expected value 0.3, so $E = 20 \times 0.3 = 6$.

quiz.prose: Deal 5 cards from a shuffled 52-card deck. The cards are drawn without replacement, so they are dependent.
quiz.question: How many aces do you expect in the hand? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each card in the hand is an ace with chance 4/52.

byKey.one-card: That is one card's chance. The hand has five cards.
byKey.four: That is how many aces the deck holds, not how many a hand expects.

explain.text: Card $k$ of the hand is an ace with chance $\tfrac{4}{52}$, so $E = 5 \times \tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac{5}{13} \approx 0.385$. Drawing without replacement makes the cards dependent; linearity does not mind.

quiz.prose: A stock rises on any given day with chance 0.53. A year has 250 trading days.
quiz.question: How many up days do you expect?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the daily chance over 250 days.

byKey.half: You treated up and down as equally likely. The chance of an up day is 0.53.

explain.text: One indicator per day, each with expected value 0.53: $E = 250 \times 0.53 = 132.5$ up days.

quiz.prose: This time 100 traders drop their cards in the bowl and each draws one at random.
quiz.question: How many traders do you expect to draw their own card?

options.why: You gave each trader a certain match. Each draws their own card with chance 1/100.
That is one trader's chance. Add it over 100 traders.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add one trader's chance over all 100.

explain.text: Each trader draws their own card with chance $\tfrac{1}{100}$, and there are 100 traders. The expected number is 1, the same as with five traders.
